title: America's Least Bad Option in Iran
gist: RAND's Cohen and Shatz argue that of three US options in the Iran war (re-escalate, walk away, or stay the course), maintaining the blockade and economic pressure campaign is the least bad, as Iran's economy implodes (rial at 2.5 million per dollar, ~90% inflation, GDP projected -7.6%). Escalation, including seizing Kharg Island, and withdrawal, which would cede Hormuz tolling to Iran, are both judged worse.

themes.theme: Costs of the US-Iran war to date

insights.claim: The US-Iran war has so far cost the United States roughly 800 casualties (15 killed, more than 800 wounded), tens of billions of dollars, hundreds of damaged base buildings, and a munitions drawdown that is straining supplies.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Munitions depletion implies sustained replenishment demand for US defense contractors.
insights.quote: So far, the Iran war has cost the United States 800 casualties, tens of billions of dollars
insights.locator: So far, the Iran war has cost

insights.claim: Fuel price increases since the start of the Iran war have pushed US inflation to a level last seen in 2023.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: War-driven energy inflation complicates the Fed's path and supports higher-for-longer rate risk.
insights.quote: Fuel prices have risen sharply since the start of the war, pushing U.S. inflation to a level last seen in 2023.
insights.locator: So far, the Iran war has cost

insights.claim: Most Americans do not believe there was sufficient reason to attack Iran, and public opposition to the war has grown over time, while even Republican supporters of the Trump administration increasingly call for ending it.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Eroding domestic support raises the probability of a policy shift, a key swing factor for oil and defense pricing.
insights.locator: So far, the Iran war has cost

insights.claim: Iran shows little sign of halting attacks on Strait of Hormuz shipping, reining in regional proxies, or curbing its nuclear program, so the conflict is not near an end.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Investors should not price a near-term reopening of Hormuz or a quick ceasefire.

themes.theme: Three strategic options and the case for staying the course

insights.claim: US policy toward Iran reduces to three options: re-escalate (full bombing or ground seizure of territory), walk away, or stay the course with blockade, economic pressure, retaliatory strikes and negotiations to reopen Hormuz and end the nuclear program.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Provides a scenario tree for mapping energy, defense and inflation outcomes.
insights.locator: In broad strokes, there are three options

insights.claim: RAND's authors argue that maintaining the blockade and pressure campaign is the strategically prudent choice, even though it is the least satisfying option and will almost certainly not produce quick results.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: The base case advocated is a prolonged, grinding standoff rather than resolution, implying persistent energy-risk premia.
insights.quote: Of the three options, this may be the least satisfying; it almost certainly will not bring quick results. But it is strategically prudent.
insights.locator: The third option is to stay

insights.claim: The authors contend time is on Washington's side because economic-pressure strategies take months or years, and Iran's fractured, hard-line regime will eventually have to compromise to avoid collapse unless it stabilizes its economy.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Signals an expected long-duration blockade, with resolution most likely via Iranian economic capitulation.
insights.quote: But time is on Washington's side.
insights.locator: The primary downside to maintaining the current

insights.claim: If Iran manages to stabilize its economy, the authors concede the United States would need to change its approach, making Iranian economic data the key trigger for a strategy shift.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Watch rial, inflation and GDP data as leading indicators of US policy change.
insights.locator: The primary downside to maintaining the current

insights.claim: The authors conclude that an imperfect option can be the right one simply because the alternatives are much worse.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Frames US policy as status-quo-sticky, lowering odds of dramatic escalation or withdrawal.
insights.quote: But sometimes an imperfect option is actually the right one—if only because the others are that much worse.
insights.locator: Sticking with the current approach is unlikely

themes.theme: Iran's economic implosion under Operation Economic Outcast

insights.claim: The Iranian rial recently traded at 2.5 million to the dollar, compared with about 630,000 to the dollar in 2024.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Signals severe balance-of-payments stress and rising regime-instability risk.
insights.quote: Its currency recently traded at 2.5 million rials to the dollar, a dramatic depreciation from about 630,000 to the dollar in 2024.
insights.locator: As messy as the conflict has been

insights.claim: Iranian inflation has recently reached almost 90 percent, with food inflation near 130 percent, unemployment is rising, and GDP this year is projected to shrink by 7.6 percent.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Hyperinflationary stress raises odds of eventual concessions or domestic upheaval.
insights.quote: Inflation has recently reached almost 90 percent, with food inflation at almost 130 percent.
insights.locator: As messy as the conflict has been

insights.claim: Iran's floating oil storage, a shadow fleet of tankers anchored outside the Strait of Hormuz that had cushioned the blockade, is now depleted, increasing pressure on the Iranian economy.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Removal of Iran's buffer stock tightens the coercive squeeze and may hasten a negotiation inflection.
insights.locator: As messy as the conflict has been

insights.claim: The authors judge that the US blockade of Iran and the wider Operation Economic Outcast are moving in the direction Washington wants despite the messiness of the conflict.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Suggests the blockade will be maintained rather than relaxed in the near term.
insights.quote: the U.S. blockade of Iran and the wider Operation Economic Outcast are going in the direction that the United States wants.
insights.locator: As messy as the conflict has been

themes.theme: Energy market impact and Hormuz flows

insights.claim: Although the US oil spot price has at times exceeded $100 per barrel, oil remains well below previous peaks on an inflation-adjusted basis.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Real oil prices suggest demand destruction is less severe than headline prices imply; upside remains if conflict escalates.
insights.quote: Although the U.S. spot price has risen above $100 per barrel at times, oil is still priced well below previous peaks once you adjust for inflation.
insights.locator: Although the U.S. spot price has risen

insights.claim: Middle Eastern crude is again flowing out of the region at near prewar levels, but LNG, refined fuels and fertilizer remain bottlenecked.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Dislocation has shifted from crude to LNG, products and fertilizer, favoring exposure to those spreads and to non-Gulf suppliers.
insights.quote: other critical commodities—liquefied natural gas, refined fuels, fertilizer—remain bottlenecked.
insights.locator: Although the U.S. spot price has risen

insights.claim: Analysts estimate it could take years to fully repair damage already done to Middle Eastern energy infrastructure, and renewed large-scale hostilities would risk further damage and higher energy prices.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Multi-year capacity impairment supports a structural energy risk premium and repair/services demand.
insights.locator: Then there is the global economic cost

insights.claim: Iran has reportedly said it wants to charge oil tankers about $1 per barrel, roughly $2 million per ship, for safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz if it controls the waterway.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: A Hormuz toll would be a permanent cost on Gulf crude shipping and a lever for future price shocks.
insights.quote: Iran has reportedly stated that it wants to charge oil tankers approximately $1 per barrel—or about $2 million per ship—for safe passage.

themes.theme: Historical track record of economic coercion

insights.claim: Economic coercion has a mixed record in producing regime change: crises preceded government change in 1980s Yugoslavia and democratization in Latin America, yet Cuba and North Korea regimes survived US pressure campaigns.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Regime-change bets on Iran are low-probability; modest negotiated outcomes are more likely.
insights.locator: To be fair, economic coercion

insights.claim: The last Iran nuclear deal shows pressure campaigns work better for modest objectives, since mounting economic duress pushed even Iranian hard-liners to negotiate; this time Iran seems less willing to concede but the pressure is more extreme.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: A negotiated deal on Hormuz and nuclear limits is a plausible endgame that would unwind energy risk premia.
insights.locator: The history of the last Iran nuclear deal

insights.claim: The authors argue a renewed full-scale air campaign is unlikely to be feasible or decisive, since air campaigns rarely topple governments and the intense opening bombardment leaves little more to achieve from the air.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Escalation is less likely to resolve the conflict quickly, so markets should not expect a decisive military end.
insights.locator: Moreover, the alternatives to staying the course

insights.claim: Regime change by ground forces would be Herculean because Iran has nearly double Iraq's population and almost quadruple its territory.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: A ground invasion would imply a massive, prolonged fiscal and defense commitment.
insights.locator: Moreover, the alternatives to staying the course

insights.claim: Despite effective bombardment from February to April, Iran retains the ability to produce missiles and drones, so escalation would likely raise US casualties and damage to bases and equipment.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Persistent Iranian strike capacity keeps regional asset and shipping risk elevated.
insights.quote: Despite the effectiveness of the bombardment from February to April, Iran still has the ability to produce missiles and drones.

insights.claim: Seizing Kharg Island, about 20 miles off Iran's coast and the hub for 90 percent of its oil exports, is feasible for the US but holding it would be costly because it sits within range of Iranian missiles and drones and air defenses are only a partial solution.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: A Kharg seizure would directly remove Iranian export capacity but risks casualties and premature withdrawal.

insights.claim: Casualties from holding Kharg Island would create political pressure for the US to abandon it prematurely, before it could force Iran into a lasting settlement.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Limited escalation options carry high reversal risk, adding volatility rather than resolution.

insights.claim: Unilaterally lifting the blockade would effectively leave the Strait of Hormuz in Iranian hands, letting Tehran tax shipping, fund the IRGC's control and proxy militias, and hold a future economic weapon while weakening US nuclear leverage.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Withdrawal would embed a structural geopolitical premium on Gulf energy transit.
insights.locator: Walking away from the war, by contrast

insights.claim: Iran has so far rejected proposals to allow free passage of exports through Hormuz in exchange for ending the blockade.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: A simple Hormuz-for-blockade deal is not currently available, lengthening the disruption timeline.
insights.locator: Walking away from the war, by contrast

insights.claim: A US withdrawal would embolden Iran to resume funding weakened proxies, worsening regional conflicts such as Yemen, the Saudi-Houthi war and attacks on Iraqi Kurdistan, which would be bad for regional stability, global energy prices and US inflation.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Withdrawal is not a clean de-escalation trade; it could raise medium-term energy and inflation risk.
insights.quote: That would be bad news for regional stability, global energy prices, and U.S. inflation.
insights.locator: Furthermore, a unilateral U.S. withdrawal

insights.claim: Iranian malign activity is global, including Hezbollah in Latin America, assassination attempts on US officials inside the US, and an alleged plot against a Royal Air Force base in Britain.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: Terror and security risk extends beyond the Gulf to Western homelands.
insights.locator: The fallout wouldn't stop there

insights.claim: A perceived Iranian victory would benefit an increasingly aligned bloc of China, Russia and North Korea, deepening Iran's drone supply and military cooperation with Russia and its energy-for-dual-use-tech ties with China.
insights.speaker: Raphael S. Cohen
insights.so_what: US withdrawal would strengthen the adversary axis, raising broader geopolitical risk premia including in Ukraine and Asia.
